variants.name: p-retry promise wrapper
variants.idiom_name: pRetry(fn, {retries, factor, minTimeout, maxTimeout, randomize, signal})
variants.implementation_notes: p-retry wraps a promise-returning or async function and owns the schedule: retries, factor and minTimeout define the capped growth (defaults 10 retries, factor 2, 1000 ms first delay), maxTimeout caps it, randomize multiplies each computed timeout by a factor between 1 and 2, and maxRetryTime bounds the total time on a monotonic clock so wall-clock adjustments cannot extend it. AbortError is the escape hatch for failures that must not be retried (a 404), and the signal option ties the loop to an AbortController so shutting down the caller stops the retries. A hand-rolled await/sleep loop is still fine for a single call site, but the wrapper is the de-facto standard and gets the details of jitter, budget and abort right.
pitfalls: The defaults are 10 retries with maxTimeout Infinity: a failing dependency is retried ten times with unbounded growth unless both are set.
p-retry aborts on most TypeErrors (network errors excepted), so wrapping a programming bug in a retryable error class reintroduces retries of bugs.
Aborting through signal stops the loop, but the in-flight operation must receive the same signal, or an abandoned attempt keeps running after the caller has given up.

variants.name: AWS SDK standard retry mode (full jitter + retry quota)
variants.idiom_name: client maxAttempts / retry_mode with the SDK's standard retry strategy
variants.implementation_notes: When the dependency is an AWS service, the SDK owns the schedule: the standard retry mode (the documented default) computes delay = random(0,1) x min(20 s, base_delay x 2^retry) - full jitter, with a 50 ms base for transient errors and a 1 s base for throttling - honours a server-directed x-amz-retry-after without adding jitter, and guards the whole thing with a retry quota token bucket so retries are suppressed during service-wide failures. Configuration is declarative (max_attempts and retry_mode through client config, AWS_MAX_ATTEMPTS/AWS_RETRY_MODE or the shared config file), so application code rarely implements the schedule; what remains is deciding which calls must not be retried and how the total request budget is enforced.
pitfalls: The retry quota is per client instance and silently stops retrying when failures are widespread, so a final error does not tell you whether retries were attempted at all.
Adaptive mode can also delay the initial request when throttling is detected, which changes the latency profile of calls that were previously never delayed.
